abstract: <jats:p>In the contemporary landscape characterized by the proliferation of big data, the implementation of robust data acquisition protocols governed by a meticulous chain of custody has become a pivotal issue. This review explores the methodologies and frameworks involved in ensuring that data acquisition processes maintain integrity, security, and authenticity throughout their lifecycle. We discuss the challenges posed by the massive volumes, velocities, and varieties of big data, and how these affect the chain of custody requirements. Additionally, we assess current technologies and practices employed to address these challenges, including blockchain integration, advanced encryption techniques, and automated provenance tracking systems. Such innovations are critical in safeguarding the trustworthiness of data used for decision-making in scientific, commercial, and legal contexts. The review concludes by identifying gaps in the current literature and suggesting future research directions aimed at enhancing the efficacy and reliability of data acquisition practices under stringent chain of custody conditions.</jats:p>
title: Data Acquisition Under Chain of Custody in the Era of Big Data

abstract: <jats:p>Introdução: A utilização de dados de saúde  em pesquisas é limitada por questões éticas. Isso desafia os pesquisadores a encontrarem formas de obter o material necessário para desenvolverem seu trabalho. Método: Usou-se uma ferramenta de Large Language Model (LLM) para gerar prontuários eletrônicos (PE) sintéticos de pacientes cardiológicos utilizando-se as técnicas "few-shot prompting" e "chain-of-thought prompting". Objetivo: criar um conjunto de dados abrangente e acessível para auxiliar no treinamento de algoritmos de classificação de texto em cenários médicos. Resultados: Foram gerados 103 PE sintéticos, abrangendo diagnósticos cardíacos distintos. Conclusão: A geração de PE sintéticos através de LLM apresentaram qualidade esperada, sendo condizentes com o conteúdo encontrado em PE reais. O conjunto de dados está disponível no repositório Zenodo para uso irrestrito pela comunidade de pesquisa, seguindo o conceito de  ciência  aberta.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>Five honest clinical crossings, no deception at any step, can still leave a patient unrecognizable to themselves. This paper asks how, and what an honest relay would require. Building on a prior analysis of the single clinical conversion, in which reflection can remain accountable to the phenomenon it transforms, this paper extends the inquiry to the multi-step relay characteristic of ordinary clinical practice: intake note, history and physical, problem list, referral, specialist impression. The single clinical conversion, from lived disturbance (S₀) to clinical rendering (S₁), was analyzed in a companion paper (Kovačić Tot 2026), which introduced methodical modesty as the tacit ideal of neutral clinical observation and established the single-crossing foundation for the HIST operator. The present manuscript extends that foundation from a single conversion to a multi-step relay chain, Sₙ = HIST(Sₙ₋₁, Cₙ), and asks a distinct question: whether local fidelity preserved at each individual link can nonetheless produce cumulative, global misrecognition across the chain as a whole.</jats:p>
                <jats:p>Drawing on Roman Ingarden's account of concretization and indeterminacy, the paper shows how legitimate local fillings-in sediment into positive findings once each concretization becomes the object of the next. Drawing on Ilya Prigogine's account of dissipative structures, it formalizes the resulting irreversibility through a hysteresis operator, showing that fidelity preserved at every local step can still fail globally across the chain. Read against Dewey's criterion that reconstruction is legitimate when it resolves the inquirer's own problematic situation, the relay is shown to displace legitimacy from patient to institution by the third link, so that reconstruction continues to satisfy Dewey's rule while no longer serving the patient whose situation began the inquiry. The paper's contribution is traceability: not restoration of the original at each step, which the clinic cannot practically deliver, but a minimal condition of provenance marking that keeps drift visible rather than silently accumulated, restoring accountability to the relay without requiring impossible fidelity to a vanishing source.</jats:p>
title: Chain of Custody: Irreversibility, Dissipation, and Traceability in the Clinical Relay

abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement and deployment of large language models (LLMs) have led to increasingly complex LLM based systems that operate as multi stage pipelines rather than isolated model instances. These systems span dataset construction, model preparation, system integration, and supporting components, together forming an end-to-end LLM supply chain (LLM-SC). In such a supply chain, threats introduced at any component may propagate downstream and upstream, ultimately compromising applications and end users. Understanding component level threats and their propagation effect across the LLM-SC is therefore essential for ensuring the trustworthiness of LLM based systems. Existing studies have examined security, privacy, and safety risks of LLMs from conceptual, stakeholder oriented, or project specific perspectives. However, a comprehensive understanding of concrete security and safety threats across the entire LLM-SC and their potential propagation paths remains in its early stages. To bridge this gap, we conduct a systematic literature review that yielded 415 academic studies and analyze security and safety threats from a supply chain perspective. We classify the identified threats according to specific LLM-SC components and examine how their impacts propagate across components through downstream and upstream paths. Based on this analysis, we provide a comprehensive overview of the LLM-SC threat landscape, identify common propagation patterns, and identify key research challenges and directions.</jats:p>
title: Security and Safety Threats in the Large Language Model Supply Chain: A Systematic Survey and Taxonomy

abstract: <jats:p>The Fairness by Design thesis is that blockchain's most significant contribution to capital markets may not be efficiency but integrity: the ability to encode fairness, accountability, and investor protection directly into the architecture itself, rather than imposing them solely through rules and ex post enforcement. Programmable smart contract custody is one of the clearest examples. The SEC's Custody Rule requires registered investment advisers to maintain client assets with a qualified custodian-an institutional intermediary whose legal status, regulatory supervision, and contractual obligations protect clients from misappropriation, commingling, and insolvency exposure. This framework has served traditional securities markets well, but its application to digital assets has in some cases produced structural gaps that the market has addressed through inefficient means. This paper argues that properly designed vaults satisfy the Custody Rule's core protective objectives through a structurally different mechanism: embedding custody constraints directly in smart contract code rather than delegating them to institutional intermediaries. Infrastructure such as vaults that satisfy defined conditions including nontransferable receipt tokens, elimination of unilateral withdrawal authority, cryptographic segregation, and continuous on-chain verifiability achieve those objectives through architectural design, enable more efficient institutional structures such as natively on-chain fund vehicles, and therefore warrant a guardrail-based compliance pathway from the SEC.</jats:p>
title: Fairness by Design, Part II: Custody by Architecture in On-Chain Markets

abstract: <jats:p>As the prominence of artificial intelligence (AI) has grown, companies are finding more ways to incorporate it into previously existing technological infrastructures to optimize their performance. Structured Query Language (SQL) is a popular way to store and retrieve data, and recently has been combined with AI search algorithms to speed up these processes. However, these successes make SQL vulnerable to attacks where malware is injected to gain access, modify, or even delete restricted data, which is also known as SQL Injection Attacks (SQLIA). This paper presents a detection approach that based on language processors, and shifts the focus of defenses against SQLIA from static pattern matching to recognizing the underlying linguistic and structural features of SQL injection attacks. Unlike traditional sanitization, this newly proposed defense will combine tokenization and vectorization with a language processor to detect malicious patterns and flag them. After running our proposed defense on a large public dataset, we received a precision score of 0.789, a recall score of 0.97, and an F1 score of 0.87 in terms of detection performance, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our defense method.</jats:p>
title: A Linguistic-based Method for SQL Injection Attack Detection and Defense

abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have made significant strides in generating coherent and contextually relevant responses across diverse domains. However, these advancements have also led to an increase in adversarial attacks, such as prompt injection, where attackers embed malicious instructions within prompts to bypass security filters and manipulate LLM outputs. Various injection techniques, including masking and encoding sensitive words, have been employed to circumvent security measures. While LLMs continuously enhance their security protocols, they remain vulnerable, particularly in multimodal contexts. This study introduces a novel method for bypassing LLM security policies by embedding malicious instructions within a mind map image. The attack leverages the intentional incompleteness of the mind map structure, specifically the absence of explanatory details. When the LLM processes the image and fills in the missing sections, it inadvertently generates unauthorized outputs, violating its intended security constraints. This approach applies to any LLM capable of extracting and interpreting text from images. Compared to the best-performing baseline method, which achieved an ASR of 30.5%, our method reaches an ASR of 90%, yielding an approximately threefold-higher attack success. Understanding this vulnerability is crucial for strengthening security policies in state-of-the-art LLMs.</jats:p>
title: Mind Mapping Prompt Injection: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks in Modern Large Language Models

abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in production systems, yet their prompt-based interaction paradigm introduces a novel attack surface encompassing prompt injection, instruction hijacking, and sensitive data leakage. This paper proposes and empirically evaluates the Secure Prompt Engineering Framework (SPEF), a four-layer, application-level defensive architecture designed to operate under black-box API conditions without requiring access to model weights or training pipelines. We conducted a controlled experiment using Llama-3.3-70B (via Groq API) with a standardized adversarial corpus of 85 test cases across six attack categories, totaling 170 model interactions (85 per condition). Results demonstrate that full SPEF deployment reduces the overall Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 17.6% to 2.4%-an 86.4% relative reduction-achieving complete mitigation (0.0% ASR) in the Indirect Injection and Role Reassignment categories. Critically, this paper documents both a failed initial implementation and the corrected version, providing a methodologically transparent account of how framework design errors were diagnosed and resolved. We further identify scorer validity as a primary methodological concern in adversarial LLM evaluation, demonstrating that naive keyword-based scoring introduces substantial false-positive contamination. All code, corpus, and raw results are released as open-source artifacts at github.com/gugacyber/spef_experiment.</jats:p>
title: Secure Prompt Engineering: A Practical Framework for Mitigating Prompt Injection and Data Leakage in LLM-based Systems

abstract: <jats:p>Today's world has seen rapid advancements in technology. With that comes even more rapid advancements in cybersecurity. And to combat that, criminals and adversaries have also developed even more advanced techniques to combat cybersecurity. Many of these techniques fall under the field of anti-forensics. Digital forensics is the branch of cybersecurity that deals with investigating incidents in cyberspace. So, to hide themselves even more, cybercriminals have come up with very created anti-forensic techniques to evade these investigators and make it harder to prove that they actually committed a crime. This paper highlights published and proven anti-forensic techniques across different devices. It covers the technical details of these techniques, as well as the forensic techniques that they evade. Although many of the techniques in this paper can be used for malicious purposes, forensic investigators should nevertheless know these so that they can continue to perform their jobs effectively despite the rapid growth of techniques that are used against them.</jats:p>
title: Anti-Forensics

abstract:
<jats:p>Anti Forensics is a collection of methods and approaches to obstruct and
avoid Digital Forensic investigations. For legal purposes, like criminal investigations or
civil lawsuits, Digital Forensics includes gathering, preserving, analyzing, and
presenting digital evidence. To make it more difficult for Forensic analysts to
reconstruct events, assign acts to particular people, or prove guilt or innocence, people
or organizations use Anti-Forensic strategies to obfuscate, distort, or delete digital
evidence. The chapter presents techniques procedures and countermeasures for digital
anti-forensics. The chapter also discusses anti-forensics ethical and legal ramifications.</jats:p>
title: Anti-forensics Techniques

abstract: <jats:p>In this day and age, it is difficult to imagine technology not being part of our everyday life. However, such can also hold the power to be used for activities that an average consumer may not partake in. This chapter focuses on anti-digital forensics and digital forensics methods. Hence, it examines detection avoidance strategies and establishes current investigation and prevention methods when a crime is committed with the help of technologies within cyberspace, reaching from device forensics to data hiding. The cases of the San Bernardino shooting, hacktivist group ‘Anonymous,' EncroChat, and the Shadowz Brotherhood are discussed, examining how offenders utilise technologies such as encryption and data wiping to try to ‘outrun' authorities as well as methods authorities implement to keep up with technological advances to prevent and detect these criminal activities.</jats:p>
title: Friend or Foe?

abstract: <jats:p>Social media forensics collects evidence from social media sites such as Facebook, WhatsApp, TikTok, and Snapchat to identify criminals. This paper discusses social media crimes such as hacking, photo morphing, shopping scams, cyberbullying, and link baiting. The paper deliberates the social media forensics techniques such as evidence collection, storing, analyzing, and preserving; the paper discusses the process of forensics examination in social media forensics. The paper examines the social media forensics tools such as WebPreserver, make a Website Hub, Pipl Search, TinEye, and TweetBeaver and discusses the applications of each device. The paper concludes by discussing the future of social media forensics.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>The growing presence of embedded systems in the daily lives of people and companies, driven by the emergence of portable devices, makes these systems ubiquitous and a valuable source of information for criminal investigations. However, the lack of resources dedicated to forensics in this context, excluding IoT devices due to their technical particularities, led to the need to start writing this material. This article seeks to introduce experts to embedded systems forensics, highlighting the importance and existence of this field, and emphasizing that microcontrollers, flash memories, ROM memories and other often overlooked devices can contain crucial evidence for solving a variety of crimes. Furthermore, it will be discussed how to adapt conventional forensic techniques to the peculiarities of embedded systems, which generally have limited processing resources, energy constraints and high connectivity, challenging traditional forensic approaches.</jats:p>
title: Hardware Forensics-an Introduction to Digital Forensics in the Embedded Computing Context

abstract: <jats:p>The exponential growth of cloud-computing infrastructures, cross-border dynamic data flows, end-to- end encrypted communication protocols, and Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems has placed digital evidence at the center of modern criminal and civil proceedings (Casey, 2011; Horsman, 2020). However, in many countries adhering to the Continental European legal tradition, including Turkey, procedural practices continue to rely on law enforcement centered legal frameworks designed for the needs of an earlier technological era (Dülger, 2022; Sieber, 2014). This structural dependence creates significant vulnerabilities with respect to institutional impartiality, equality of arms (armes égales), the integrity of the chain of custody, and compliance with fundamental rights (European Court of Human Rights, 1993; Carrier, 2005). To address these systemic bottlenecks, this study proposes a comprehensive legislative framework: a Draft Digital Forensics Act and an autonomous Digital Forensics Authority (DFA) endowed with public legal personality, to be established under the proposed legislation (Demirci, 2026). Evaluated in light of the Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest Convention), the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and ISO/IEC 27037 standards (ISO & IEC, 2012; European Parliament & Council of the European Union, 2016), the proposed model seeks to align complex digital investigations with the right to a fair trial guaranteed by Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) (European Court of Human Rights, 1993; Trechsel, 2006) through standardized technical procedures, statutory safeguards designed to retain qualified specialists within the public sector (Garfinkel, 2010), and a technical review mechanism for expert opinions submitted by the parties (Taruffo, 2003).</jats:p>
title: Rethinking Digital Forensics Governance in the Continental European Legal System: A Proposed Statutory Model for an Independent Digital Forensics Authority

abstract: <jats:p>A sequence of three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is conducted to support a small online business' decision of whether and how to implement AI in the creation of email marketing content. Recent developments in frequentist statistical decision theory are used to accommodate small samples available for testing in the small-business setting. The RCTs comprise three test policy cells with email content created by (i) salaried writers ("human''), (ii) a large-language model ("LLM''), and (iii) a "hybrid'' combination of a human editing the content created by the LLM, respectively. When a "no email'' control policy is included, all three test cells approximately double the gross profits from orders relative to the control cell. The RCTs vary whether the hybrid cell is edited by a salaried writer or the marketing team. The LLM cells vary whether the AI is pre-trained using historic emails or uses a prompt-based generative pre-trained transformer ("GPT''). Decision theory always selects one of the AI cells over the standard human policy on the basis of total annual profit net of related labor and software overhead.</jats:p>
title: Large Language Models and Creative Content Design: A Case Study of Email Marketing at Wine Access

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The present study is a comparative production study which investigates the effect of L1 email pragmatics on L2 email performance and examines the extent to which the L2 email production of advanced, Greek learners of English shows agreement with their L1 email production. The study identified culture-specific pragmatic norms and aspects of L1 pragmatic behaviours that learners transferred to their L2 emails. A preference for formality and direct strategies was confirmed in both data sets suggesting that the learners’ emails converge with those of NS of Greek and approximate native Greek norms. Results further pointed towards a high degree of agreement in the majority of the modifiers employed by the two groups.</jats:p>
title: The effect of first language pragmatics on second language email performance

abstract: <jats:p>Writing formal emails requires clarity, conciseness, and accuracy. Many English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners find these skills challenging. Large Language Models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, represent a significant advancement in natural language processing. However, their effectiveness in structured, task-specific language tasks for education is not well studied. This study investigates whether the GPT-3.5 model can assist EFL students in writing formal emails with greater precision and structural accuracy. The research treats the classroom as a real-world test case for the model’s abilities. It applied a quasi-experimental method. Data were collected from control and experimental groups (N = 60). The study used a test and semi-structured interviews. The results show ChatGPT improved formal email writing among EFL students. Qualitative findings highlight the tool’s ease of use and time-saving nature. ChatGPT also boosts clarity and confidence. Some concerns about overreliance on ChatGPT emerge. The tool sometimes struggled with subject lines, sign-offs, and signatures. This suggests that human intervention is needed. Contributing to AI-assisted pedagogy, this study shows how ChatGPT can improve EFL students' formal email writing skills.</jats:p>
title: Leveraging A Large Language Model for Precision Enhancement in EFL Email Writing: A Quasi-Experimental Study

abstract: In High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments, a comprehensive understanding of cybersecurity threats and their underlying attack strategies is essential. However, current research predominantly focuses on maliciousness determination, typically emphasizing the code's operational behaviors rather than the attack strategies employed. The advancements in multimedia computing, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), have paved the way for innovative solutions to the aforementioned bottleneck. This work proposes MalGTA (Guided Malware Tactical Analysis), an LLM-based system that automates ATT\&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge)-aligned malware tactical analysis through Cuckoo Sandbox-driven dynamic profiling. Specifically, we construct a multi-source knowledge base integrated with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which mitigates hallucinations in LLMs through context-sensitive threat intelligence retrieval. In addition, we propose a query optimization strategy to address challenges related to input information overload and attention dispersion in LLMs, enabling context-aware data refinement from Cuckoo reports. Finally, this study conducts dynamic analysis on classical VirusShare and Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) samples and constructs an evaluation dataset based on the authoritative malware analysis platform HybridAnalysis. Experimental results show the effectiveness of the method.
title: MalGTA: Large language Model-based Guided Malware Tactical Analysis

abstract: Malware reverse engineering, the process of dissecting malicious software to understand its functionality and behavior, faces significant challenges due to the complexity and obfuscation techniques employed by modern malware. The application of Gemini Pro for interpreting reverse-engineered malware code introduces a novel and significant approach to enhancing the understanding of complex malware behaviors. By leveraging advanced natural language processing capabilities, the model provides detailed and accurate explanations of malware's functional components, offering substantial improvements over traditional analysis methods. The study demonstrates the model's proficiency in identifying key operational mechanisms and recommending relevant indicators of compromise, which are crucial for effective threat detection and mitigation. A comprehensive comparative analysis reveals that Gemini Pro outperforms conventional static and dynamic analysis tools in terms of clarity, coherence, and time efficiency. Detailed case studies of various malware samples, including Ramnit, Kelihos, and Lollipop, illustrate the model's ability to generate clear and actionable insights, thereby facilitating better decision-making in cybersecurity contexts. The findings underscore the potential of integrating advanced natural language processing models into cybersecurity workflows to significantly enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of malware analysis and mitigation efforts.
title: Malware Reverse Engineering with Large Language Model for Superior Code Comprehensibility and IoC Recommendations

abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancements in cyber-attack strategies are in parallel with the measures for detection, analysis, and prevention. Attackers have recently developed fileless malware that can simply bypass existing security mechanisms. Researchers publish reports to help discover fileless malware and to better understand the threatʼs scope to counteract it. However, with the lack of studies on fileless malware regarding the classification and the scale of the threat, they have not been thoroughly analyzed. As a result, in this research, we explored the most recent advancements in fileless malware prevention and detection and highlighted future research challenges. We also propose an analytical approach based on the attack strategies and attributes of the selected sample. The results of the approach demonstrate that the proposed fileless malware technique is a viable protection mechanism.</jats:p>
title: Fileless Malware Threats: Recent Advances, Analysis Approach Through Memory Forensics and Research Challenges

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Malware family classification is crucial for threat detection, yet existing methods struggle with generalization, multi-task adaptability, and interpretability. We propose VIMAR, a unified vision–language model that supports classification, similarity detection, and open-world analysis via explanation-rich supervision and a two-stage training pipeline. On the Malimg dataset, VIMAR achieves 94.2% accuracy in family classification, surpassing the best CNN baseline by +3.1%. It also attains 85.2% and 88.0% accuracy in zero-shot and few-shot settings, significantly outperforming vision–language baselines. Moreover, its reasoning outputs align well with human judgments. The codebase and scripts will be released to the community.</jats:p>
title: VIMAR: vision-language informed malware analysis and reasoning model

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The increasing sophistication and polymorphic nature of malware necessitate intelligent, adaptive forensic frameworks that go beyond static rule-based detection. In particular, the traditional techniques for evidence collection and analysis would not catch the evolving behaviors of advanced malware, lack context-aware feature weighting, and fail to maintain accuracy under concept drifts or temporal drifts. Such limitations thus also impede timely threats attribution and malware family discovery processes. To bridge these gaps, we propose an iterative framework for evidence collection and malware activity analysis by utilizing machine learning and explainable AI paradigms. The framework integrates five newly proposed modules: (1) DynaTrace-XAI employs SHAP-based attribution for real-time reweighting of forensic features, dynamically enhancing the significance of impactful indicators in the process. (2) TempNet V introduces temporal ensemble validation at daily, weekly, and monthly levels, deploying heterogeneous models (e.g. LSTM, RF) to counter data drifts dependent on time. (3) GRAFIN-A reconstructs execution traces into behavior graphs through Graph Attention Networks, which are then subjected to unsupervised clustering with DBSCAN and anomaly detection through graph similarity scoring methods. (4) RiskActive-L blends anomaly-derived risk scores with model uncertainty to prioritize more unlabeled high-risk samples within an active learning loop, strongly improving data labeling efficiency. (5) DriftMon-F implements a forensic-context-aware drift detection mechanism via KL divergence and meta-log correlation to trigger timely retraining in the event of contextual shifts. In concert, these modules constitute a closed-loop system whereby evidence assignment, model validation, clustering, sample selection, and drift handling processes become continuously refined. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the empirical achievements: 15% increase in F1-score, 23% gain in variant detection, reduction of 45% in labeling effort, and 70% reduction in drift recovery lag, leading to considerable advances in adaptive malware forensics.</jats:p>
title: Design of an improved validation model with dynamic attribution and graph-based anomaly analysis for malware forensics

abstract: <jats:p>In day to day life, the internet is becoming an essential part for making use of services like online banking or advertising. On the internet, just as in the real world, there are those who wish to harm others by taking advantage of trustworthy individuals anytime whenever money is exchanged. For accomplishing their goals, people intent with malicious software to harm the internet and this attack is named as Malware. The malware denotes as malevolent software which is installed in computer or mobile without awareness of owner or user. As a result, by looking into this malicious software, the IT team is better able to assess a security incident and help stop more infections from spreading to the victim's computer or server. For this kind of performance, IT responders typically look for solutions known technically as malware forensics. The importance of malware forensics has grown as the cybercrime community targets financial institutions, technological companies, and retail businesses with malicious software. This virus can be broken down into two categories: static malware and dynamic malware. While dynamic malware analysis offers various tools and code, static malware analysis has several limitations. As a result, dynamic malware analysis is often preferred in most contexts. This chapter deals with the study of malware types, how it is affecting the users, static malware limitations, and dynamic malware tools that are used for analyzing malicious software. Further focuses on issues, challenges that are facing in malware analysis and available online malware analysis tools that work on cloud along with feature research prospects.</jats:p>
title: Malware Forensics Analysis and Detection in Cyber Physical Systems

abstract: <jats:p>Evaluating log summarization systems is challenging due to the lack of high-quality reference summaries and the limitations of existing metrics like ROUGE and BLEU, which depend on surface-level lexical overlap. We introduce REFLEX, a reference-free evaluation metric for log summarization based on large language model (LLM) judgment. REFLEX uses LLMs as zero-shot evaluators to assess summary quality along dimensions such as relevance, informativeness, and coherence, without requiring gold-standard references or human annotations. We show that REFLEX produces stable, interpretable, and finegrained evaluations across multiple log summarization dataset, and more effectively distinguishes model outputs than traditional metrics. REFLEX provides a scalable alternative for evaluating log summaries in real-world settings where reference data is scarce or unavailable.</jats:p>
title: REFLEX: Reference-Free Evaluation of Log Summarization via Large Language Model Judgment

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Software systems generate massive, evolving, semi-structured logs that are central to reliability engineering and AIOps, yet difficult to analyze at scale under drift and limited labels. Recent advances in pretrained Transformer models and instructiontuned large language models (LLMs) have reshaped log analysis by enabling semantic generalization and cross-source evidence integration, but also introducing deployment risks such as context limits, latency and cost, privacy constraints, and
hallucinations. This paper presents
                    <jats:bold>LLM4Log</jats:bold>
                    , a systematic review of LLM-based log analysis across the end-to-end pipeline, from upstream logging-statement generation and maintenance to log parsing/structuring and downstream tasks including anomaly detection, failure prediction, root cause analysis, and log summarization. Following a structured search and manual screening protocol, we completed literature collection in November 2025 and identified 145 unique papers across seven logging tasks. We organize the research area through a unified, task-driven taxonomy, summarize common design patterns (prompting/ICL, retrieval grounding, fine-tuning, tool/agent augmentation, and verification), and analyze evaluation practices, datasets, metrics, and reproducibility. Based on these cross-paper analyses, we summarize key lessons and open challenges for reliable real-world adoption. We emphasize robustness under drift and long-tail events, grounding and faithfulness for operator-facing outputs, and deployment-oriented designs with verifiable behavior.
                  </jats:p>
title: LLM4Log: A Systematic Review of Large Language Model-based Log Analysis

abstract: <jats:p>Web log data analysis is essential for monitoring and securing modern software systems. However, traditional manual analysis methods struggle to cope with the rapidly growing volumes and complexity of log data, resulting in inefficiencies and potential security risks. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an AI-driven log analysis framework utilizing advanced natural language processing techniques from large language models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT. The framework aims to automate log data normalization, anomaly detection, and risk assessment, enabling the real-time identification and mitigation of security threats. Our objectives include reducing dependency on human analysis, enhancing the accuracy and speed of threat detection, and providing a scalable solution suitable for diverse web service environments. Through extensive experimentation with realistic log scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in swiftly identifying and responding to web-based security threats, ultimately improving both security posture and operational efficiency.</jats:p>
title: An AI-Based Risk Analysis Framework Using Large Language Models for Web Log Security

abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a novel approach to intelligent log management, using large language models (LLMs) to detect and resolve anomalies in real-time. By extending the capabilities of a model like GPT for log analysis, we can enable the automatic detection of anomalies with actionable recommendations. The model was trained on a dataset of system logs with hyperparameters optimized for anomaly detection accuracy. The evaluation shows that the model successfully identified 85% of anomalies with a false positive rate of 5%, significantly outperforming traditional log analysis tools. Further, the model provides actionable recommendations in 90% of cases, which reduce the Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR) by 40%.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Engineering applications of artificial intelligence require systems that are not only accurate in prediction, but also deployable, auditable and robust across complete engineering workflows. This paper presents Auto-Logging, a domain-grounded large language model agent framework for physics-constrained well-log interpretation. The artificial intelligence contribution is a Planner-Executor agent architecture that separates workflow reasoning from numerical prediction: the Planner converts a user request into a dependency-aware interpretation plan by retrieving petrophysical procedures and physical rules, whereas the Executor invokes registered preprocessing tools and task-specific models through standardized interfaces and returns structured status, metrics and alarms. The engineering application is end-to-end subsurface well-log interpretation, including curve quality control, preprocessing, missing-curve imputation, lithology classification, reservoir-parameter prediction, fluid judgment and report generation. On a forward-simulated data set and a public well-log prediction benchmark, Auto-Logging completes single-well interpretation in 10.2--25.3 min, compared with approximately 14 h for expert-assisted conventional interpretation, while reducing manual intervention to about 1 min and maintaining competitive prediction performance. Ablation studies show that retrieval-augmented domain grounding, dynamic agent scheduling and structured feedback each improve workflow reliability. These results demonstrate a practical artificial intelligence system for engineering workflow automation, in which language models coordinate validated numerical components under explicit physical constraints rather than replacing domain models or expert review.</jats:p>
title: Auto-Logging: domain-grounded large language model agents for physics-constrained well-log interpretation workflows

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Public facing large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health guidance, including triage recommendations. We evaluated whether augmenting LLM prompts with standardized clinical concepts from the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) could improve the safety and robustness of clinical triage recommendations.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We used a publicly available dataset comprising 60 clinician-authored clinical vignettes, each represented in 16 demographic and narrative variations, yielding 960 vignette-factor combinations. Clinical entities were extracted using a two-stage pipeline combining ClinicalBERT-based named entity recognition with rule-based identification of laboratory abnormalities. Extracted entities were mapped to UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs).Negated concepts were excluded. A confidence-weighted CUI voting classifier was trained using empirical associations between CUIs and clinician-assigned triage categories. We compared five approaches: CUI-only classification, MedGemma 27B, MedGemma 27B augmented with CUIs, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-4o-mini augmented with CUIs. Outcomes included overall accuracy, under-triage, over-triage, emergency-case accuracy, and sensitivity to anchoring statements.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>CUI augmentation decreased under-triage but increased over-triage in both models tested (GPT-4o-mini and MedGemma 27B). It improved high-acuity recognition while reducing recognition of low-acuity cases. CUI augmentation had mixed effects on overall triage accuracy; accuracy increased for MedGemma 27B but decreased for GPT-4o-mini. Emergency-case accuracy improved from 73.0% to 80.7% for GPT-4o-mini and from 60.5% to 68.5% for MedGemma 27B. CUI augmentation also reduced susceptibility to anchoring statements. These findings suggest that the principal value of CUI augmentation may be shifting model behavior toward safety-oriented behavior rather than uniformly improving overall accuracy.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ontology-grounded prompt augmentation shifted LLM triage recommendations toward greater sensitivity to high-acuity presentations and reduced overall under-triage. These safety gains were accompanied by increased over-triage and mixed effects on overall accuracy. A hybrid architecture combining LLM-based language understanding with interpretable UMLS-derived clinical concepts may improve the safety and robustness of AI-assisted triage. Further evaluation using real-world patient communications and clinical outcomes is warranted.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
title: Reducing Under-Triage Risk in Large Language Model Based Clinical Triage Using UMLS-CUI Augmentation

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Stroke is a time-sensitive neurological emergency in which early EMS activation and presentation to definitive care are cornerstones of effective therapy. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted by the public for medical advice, but the veracity of the guidance provided by commercially available models responding to potential stroke symptoms is not well understood.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We performed a cross-model benchmarking study comparing the triage choices of three frontier LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, and Llama 3.3-70b-versatile) on first-person vignettes describing a unilateral arm symptom on waking, across 10 symptom descriptors, and two clinical phases (before and after a partially reassuring self-examination), with or without a clinical distractor (n=50 per condition).</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Claude sought emergency care most often, Llama least, and GPT-4o in between, diverging most sharply in the post-examination phase where Claude called 911 in 100% of runs, Llama called for non-emergency help in 100%, and GPT-4o was symptom-dependent. A distractor shifted behavior away from emergency care in almost all conditions: calling 911 fell from 37.9% to 14.6% and waiting rose from 0% to 45.9% in the post-examination vignette. Responses were also sensitive to symptom word: weak, limp, heavy, and clumsy generated higher alarm, whereas numb, tingly, odd, strange, and weird generated less urgent responses.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The increasing use of LLMs for medical advice has significant public health implications. Commercially available LLMs show significant model-to-model variability and framing sensitivity when confronted with potential stroke symptoms, including under-recognition of canonical CDC warning descriptors, underscoring the need for systematic benchmarking as these tools become de facto first points of contact for patients experiencing neurological emergencies.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
title: Cross-Model Variability in Large Language Model Triage Behavior for Potential Stroke Symptoms

To evaluate whether prompt structure changes large language model-recommended triage in urologic patient messages and whether safety-focused prompting reduces unsafe undertriage without increasing overtriage. Methods. In this scenario-based, cross-sectional, comparative study, 50 synthetic urologic patient messages were tested in three prompt arms: a neutral base prompt (P1), a red-flag-focused prompt (P2), and a safety- and triage-calibration-focused prompt (P3). This yielded 150 first-response outputs in Turkish from GPT-5.4 Thinking. For each case, two urologists predefined the gold-standard triage level and required core warnings. Primary outcomes were complete concordance, unsafe undertriage, and overtriage; omission of critical warnings was secondary. Results. Complete concordance was 45/50 (90.0%) in P1, 42/50 (84.0%) in P2, and 41/50 (82.0%) in P3. No unsafe undertriage or omission of critical warnings occurred in any arm. Overtriage was 2/50 (4.0%) in P1, 8/50 (16.0%) in P2, and 9/50 (18.0%) in P3. Compared with P1, overtriage was significantly higher in P2 and P3 (p = 0.031 and p = 0.016, respectively), with no difference between P2 and P3. Conclusion. In this dataset, safety-focused prompting did not improve unsafe undertriage but increased overtriage. Evaluations of patient-facing artificial intelligence should therefore assess not only red-flag recognition but also whether the recommended level of care is appropriate.
title: Effect of Prompt Structure on Large Language Model-Recommended Triage Levels in Urologic Patient Messages

abstract:
<ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>Abstract</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>Triaging is a crucial process within emergency departments (EDs), designed to prioritize patients based on the urgency of their condition. It relies heavily on both numerical vital parameters and descriptive triage notes. However, triage decisions are often influenced by local disease patterns, demographic variations, and institutional guidelines, making the process context-dependent. Despite this, existing triage training programs are largely generic and fail to represent the local uniqueness of clinical practice.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>This study proposes an Artificial Intelligence (AI) based approach to develop a hospital-specific triage prediction model using a Large Language Model (LLM) architecture. The AI model learns directly from local triage data, allowing it to simulate real-world triage decision-making patterns. The trained model will be integrated into a self-directed, scenario-based online triage training program hosted on a Moodle platform. The program aims to provide learners with AI-generated feedback, bridging the gap between conventional training and localized, data-driven education.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>1. Introduction</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>Emergency triage plays a pivotal role in ensuring timely patient care. It involves assessing the severity of a patient’s condition and assigning an appropriate triage category, typically ranging from Level 1 (resuscitation) to Level 5 (non-urgent) according to the Australasian Triage Scale (ATS). The accuracy and consistency of triage decisions are vital for optimizing patient outcomes and resource allocation in busy emergency settings.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>Traditional triage training programs rely on standardized case studies and manual instruction, which may not fully reflect the variations in regional disease prevalence, patient demographics, and institutional protocols. These differences can significantly influence how triage nurses interpret patient symptoms and vital signs. Consequently, healthcare professionals often require additional localized training to achieve optimal decision-making accuracy within their own clinical environments.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>Artificial Intelligence has demonstrated increasing potential in modeling complex clinical reasoning. By learning from real-world data, AI can emulate human decision-making and highlight underlying patterns that may not be evident through conventional rule-based systems. This study leverages machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) techniques to develop a predictive triage model capable of reproducing the decision logic specific to a single hospital. The model then serves as the foundation for an adaptive self-directed training platform.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>2. Objectives</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>
                  The primary objectives of this study were to:
                  <ns3:list list-type="order">
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Develop a machine learning–based triage prediction model using real hospital data that includes both vital signs and triage notes.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Evaluate and compare multiple algorithms to identify the model with the best accuracy and interpretability.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Integrate the model into a self-directed triage training platform that provides learners with real-time, AI-generated feedback and explanations.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Demonstrate how AI can support region-specific clinical education, bridging the gap between generalized and localized triage training.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                  </ns3:list>
                  <ns3:bold>3. Methods</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>3.1 Data Collection</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>The dataset comprised three years of anonymized triage records collected from a metropolitan hospital in Victoria, Australia. Each record included structured numerical data such as blood pressure, oxygen saturation, heart rate, and temperature, and unstructured text data from triage notes that describe the patient’s presenting complaint and the nurse’s initial observations. All data were de-identified before analysis to ensure compliance with privacy and ethical standards.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>3.2 Data Preprocessing</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>Data preprocessing involved cleaning and standardizing numerical features, managing missing values, and normalizing outlier ranges. The free-text triage notes were processed using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, including tokenization, lemmatization, and the creation of Word2Vec embeddings to transform clinical text into numerical representations that capture semantic meaning.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>3.3 Model Development</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>Eight machine learning and deep learning models were developed and evaluated for triage level prediction. These models incorporated both structured and unstructured clinical inputs, combining vital parameters (e.g., blood pressure, oxygen saturation, heart rate) with triage notes describing the patient’s presenting complaint and initial nurse observations.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  The following models were implemented and tested:
                  <ns3:list list-type="bullet">
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Logistic Regression</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Random Forest</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with GloVe embeddings</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with BioBERT embeddings</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with BERT embeddings</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>FCDNN (Fully Connected Deep Neural Network) with GPT-2 embeddings</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Voting model combining Logistic Regression and Random Forest predictions</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Voting model combining Gradient Boosting and Random Forest predictions</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                  </ns3:list>
                  The deep learning models utilized pre-trained word embeddings (GloVe, BioBERT, BERT, and GPT-2) to extract semantic and contextual information from the triage notes, enhancing the model’s ability to interpret complex clinical language.
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>To ensure transparency and clinical interpretability, Explainable AI (XAI) techniques were applied using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP analysis quantified the relative contribution of each input feature, including vital signs and key terms within triage notes, to the model’s final prediction. This process enabled visualization of how specific clinical variables influenced triage decisions and confirmed that the model’s reasoning aligned with expert clinical judgment.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>The combination of high predictive accuracy and explainability made the Random Forest + SHAP pipeline the most suitable candidate for integration into the self-directed triage training platform, ensuring both performance and interpretability for real-world educational use.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>3.4 Model Evaluation</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>The models were validated using stratified sampling and evaluated based on precision, recall, and F1-score metrics to ensure balanced performance across all triage levels.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>To ensure clinical reliability, a real-world validation framework was designed in collaboration with three official triage officers from the hospital. Together, we developed a structured test framework consisting of 10 anonymized triage cases that represented a range of clinical scenarios and triage levels. The officers independently reviewed these cases, and their assessments were used as the reference standard for validating model predictions.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>4. Results and Analysis</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>The Random Forest model demonstrated the best performance among all algorithms tested, achieving the following results:</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  The Random Forest model achieved:
                  <ns3:list list-type="bullet">
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>
                        <ns3:bold>F1-score:</ns3:bold>
                        0.85
                      </ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>
                        <ns3:bold>Overall accuracy:</ns3:bold>
                        87 %
                      </ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>
                        <ns3:bold>Category 2 accuracy:</ns3:bold>
                        82 %
                      </ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>
                        <ns3:bold>Category 1 accuracy:</ns3:bold>
                        64 %
                      </ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                  </ns3:list>
                  The lower performance for Category 1 cases reflects their rarity and complexity, suggesting that additional high-acuity data could further enhance accuracy.
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>The findings indicate that AI can effectively learn the decision-making patterns underlying clinical triage. </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>
                  Real-world testing confirmed the model’s reliability in replicating hospital-specific triage behavior. Importantly, this result supports the broader hypothesis that
                  <ns3:bold>each hospital can train its own triage model</ns3:bold>
                  using local data, thereby preserving the individuality of its patient population and clinical workflows.
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>5. Integration into a Self-directed Training Platform</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>Building on these results, the study’s second phase involves developing a scenario-based self-learning platform hosted on Moodle. In this platform, healthcare trainees will be presented with realistic triage cases derived from the dataset. After selecting an appropriate triage level, their decision will be compared with the AI model’s predicted “ideal” triage level and explanation.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  The system provides immediate feedback that includes:
                  <ns3:list list-type="bullet">
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>A rationale generated by the AI model, describing which clinical features influenced the decision.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Comparison with expert-validated triage categories.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Progress tracking and adaptive difficulty adjustment to personalize learning.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                  </ns3:list>
                  This approach offers a scalable and data-driven solution for ongoing triage education, particularly in resource-constrained environments where access to in-person training may be limited.
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>6. Discussion</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>The study demonstrates that AI can replicate and explain hospital-specific triage patterns with a satisfactory level of accuracy. By combining vital parameters and narrative triage notes, the model bridges quantitative and qualitative aspects of clinical reasoning. Unlike static rule-based systems, the AI model learns dynamically from historical data, ensuring that it reflects real local practices.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  From an educational perspective, integrating such models into training systems promotes self-directed learning, enabling healthcare professionals to independently practice and refine their clinical judgment. Moreover, explainable AI (XAI) methods, such as feature importance and SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), can further enhance learner understanding by showing
                  <ns3:italic>why</ns3:italic>
                  the model prioritized specific features.
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>This framework can be adapted for different hospitals and regions worldwide. Each institution could train its own localized AI model using its internal triage data while maintaining privacy and security through anonymization. As more datasets are incorporated, these models could form the basis for national or regional triage training standards that balance consistency with contextual relevance.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>7. Limitations</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>
                  While the results are promising, several limitations must be acknowledged:
                  <ns3:list list-type="bullet">
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>The dataset was limited to a single metropolitan hospital, which may restrict generalizability.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Category 1 (critical) cases were underrepresented, affecting accuracy for high-acuity predictions.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>The model has not yet been deployed in a live training environment; educational impact will be evaluated in the next phase.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Natural language variations and abbreviations in triage notes can introduce interpretation challenges, which future iterations may address using larger LLM architectures or domain-specific embeddings.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                  </ns3:list>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>8. Future Work</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>
                  The next phase of research will involve:
                  <ns3:list list-type="order">
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Deploying the Moodle-based system for pilot testing among triage trainees.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Collecting user feedback to evaluate the educational effectiveness of AI-generated feedback.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Expanding the dataset to include additional hospitals to assess cross-institutional adaptability.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                    <ns3:list-item>
                      <ns3:p>Integrating Explainable AI techniques (e.g., SHAP, LIME) to improve transparency and learner engagement.</ns3:p>
                    </ns3:list-item>
                  </ns3:list>
                  Long-term, the goal is to develop a federated triage learning ecosystem where hospitals can train, validate, and share anonymized model weights, accelerating triage education globally while safeguarding patient data.
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p/>
                <ns3:p>
                  <ns3:bold>9. Conclusion</ns3:bold>
                </ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>This study successfully demonstrates that Artificial Intelligence can capture and reproduce the clinical reasoning patterns unique to individual hospitals. The Random Forest model achieved strong performance in predicting triage levels using combined vital parameters and triage notes. More importantly, the methodology can be adapted to any healthcare institution to generate its own hospital-specific triage model.</ns3:p>
                <ns3:p>By integrating this AI capability into a self-directed online learning environment, the project bridges the gap between generic training programs and context-aware clinical education. This represents a meaningful advancement toward personalized medical learning, where technology enhances, not replaces, human expertise.</ns3:p>
title: Developing a large language model for a self-directed triage training program using artificial intelligence

abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in health-related interactions in which their outputs may influence clinical judgment and action, yet existing validation approaches do not fully capture how decision authority is distributed across the human–AI workflow. We conceptualize decision-authority placement (DAP) as a configuration-level, safety-critical construct linking workflow, intended use, and validation in LLM-mediated triage, and specify its four constitutive, assessable dimensions. Unlike classifications of decision authority at the deployment level, DAP assesses whether practical authority enacted in use corresponds to, or diverges from, its intended placement. Grounded in established accounts of how authority is organized in interaction, and informed by a focused illustrative overview of intended-use validation, human–AI decision support, automation, decision-authority concepts, and LLM triage-adjacent evaluations, DAP comprises four constitutive dimensions: output status, task-specific user competence, delegated decision function, and action closure. These dimensions specify how practical authority over triage-relevant functions is assigned, constrained, or displaced across human–LLM interaction and workflow. Comparative application across three plausible triage configurations shows that similar LLM functions can have different safety implications depending on where authority is placed. Accuracy and output-performance remain necessary, but their safety meaning depends on the configuration in which LLM outputs are interpreted and translated into action. Validation should therefore move beyond model outputs alone and assess the human–LLM configuration through which decision authority is enacted across users, tasks, and care pathways.</jats:p>
title: Who Really Decides in Large Language Model-Mediated Triage? The Placement of Decision Authority Across the Human-AI Workflow

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Accurate medical decision-making is critical for both patients and clinicians. Patients often struggle to interpret their symptoms, determine their severity, and select the right specialist. Simultaneously, clinicians face challenges in integrating complex patient data to make timely, accurate diagnoses. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to bridge this gap by supporting decision-making for both patients and healthcare providers. In this study, we benchmark multiple LLM versions and an LLM-based workflow incorporating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on a curated dataset of 2,000 medical cases derived from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care database. Our findings show that these LLMs are capable of providing personalized insights into likely diagnoses, suggesting appropriate specialists, and assessing urgent care needs. These models may also support clinicians in refining diagnoses and decision-making, offering a promising approach to improving patient outcomes and streamlining healthcare delivery.</jats:p>

abstract:
BACKGROUND

Mass-casualty and operational triage require rapid decisions under uncertainty, yet real-world labeled decision data from these settings are scarce, heterogeneous, and difficult to collect at scale. Immersive virtual reality (VR) simulation provides a controlled way to generate structured human triage data in realistic high-consequence scenarios.

 OBJECTIVE

To evaluate whether simulation-derived human triage examples improve the performance and safety profile of a lightweight open-weight large language model (LLM) beyond zero-shot prompting and explicit triage guidance alone, and whether the pattern is observed in simulation datasets organized around Sort, Assess, Life-Saving Interventions, Treatment/Transport (SALT) and Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC).

 METHODS

We performed a retrospective computational evaluation using structured cases derived from immersive VR triage simulations. Four prompting conditions were evaluated: zero-shot, context/guideline only, simulation-derived few-shot examples only, and few-shot examples plus context. In the TCCC-oriented analysis, few-shot examples were evaluated from both a matched TCCC-derived source and a cross-source SALT-derived source mapped to the four TCCC labels. Outcomes included accuracy; F1 score, which balances precision and recall, summarized as macro-F1 and weighted-F1; per-category F1; under-triage; critical under-triage; pooled failure modes; attribute-stratified performance; few-shot sensitivity; and prompt-elicited model confidence. TCCC row-level evaluations contain repeated presentations and are interpreted descriptively.

 RESULTS

For SALT, test accuracy was 68.2% with zero-shot prompting, 68.4% with context alone, 71.1% with few-shot examples, and 79.1% with few-shot plus context; macro-F1 was 51.7%, 57.2%, 70.7%, and 83.8%, respectively. In TCCC, few-shot-plus-context accuracy was 87.0% with matched-source examples and 88.1% with cross-source examples; the corresponding context-only accuracies were 68.6% and 70.9%. The gain from adding examples beyond context alone was 10.7 percentage points for SALT, 18.5 points for matched-source TCCC, and 17.2 points for cross-source TCCC (pooled descriptive gain, 17.8 points). Category-level results showed large gains for EXPECTANT with simulation examples, while SALT DELAYED remained the weakest category. SALT critical under-triage decreased from 11.1% with few-shot prompting to 0.4% with few-shot plus context. TCCC under-triage decreased from 9.8% to 5.5% in the matched-source analysis and from 9.8% to 4.9% in the cross-source analysis; critical under-triage was 0% in both few-shot-plus-context source conditions. Prompt-elicited confidence remained high even when predictions were wrong and did not provide a reliable case-level safety filter.

 CONCLUSIONS

Simulation-derived human examples improved lightweight LLM triage performance beyond explicit framework guidance alone. The effect was observed with both matched-source TCCC examples and cross-source SALT-derived examples, and the strongest conditions reduced safety-relevant under-triage. These findings support immersive simulation as a practical source of reusable human decision data that preserve observed variation and experiential judgments not necessarily encoded in written guidance or reproduced by model-generated synthetic cases, with potential relevance to other high-consequence domains where real-world decision data are scarce. TCCC estimates are descriptive because many rows are repeated presentations of a much smaller number of patient identities, and the results do not establish readiness for autonomous or real-time clinical triage.
title: Simulation-Derived Human Triage Data Improve Lightweight Large Language Model Performance in Mass-Casualty and Tactical Triage: A Multi-Dataset Prompting Study (Preprint)

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Purpose: Ophthalmic triage is challenging for non-specialists due to limited training and rising global eye disease burden. This study evaluates a multimodal frame-work integrating clinical text and ophthalmic imaging with large language models (LLMs). Hallucination detection and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning were incorporated to improve diagnostic accuracy. Methods: A dataset of 41 ophthalmology cases from a Singapore restructured hospital was pre-processed with acronym expansion, sentence re-construction, and hallucination detection. To address dataset size limitations, 100 syn-thetic cases were generated via one-shot GPT-4 prompting, validated by semantic checks and ophthalmologist review. Three diagnostic approaches were tested: Text-Only, Im-age-Assisted, and Image with CoT. Diagnostic performance was quantified using SNOMED-CT mapping and a dissimilarity score reflecting semantic distance between predicted and reference diagnoses. Results: The synthetic dataset included anterior seg-ment (n=40), posterior segment (n=35), and extraocular (n=25) cases. The text-only ap-proach yielded a mean dissimilarity of 6.353 +/- 1.685. Incorporation of image assistance reduced this to 5.234 +/- 1.305, while CoT prompting provided further gains when imag-ing cues were ambiguous. Conclusions: The multimodal pipeline improved diagnostic alignment in ophthalmology triage. Image inputs enhanced accuracy, and CoT reasoning reduced errors from ambiguous features, supporting its potential as an accurate tool for ophthalmology triage.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating a Multi-Modal Large Language Model for Ophthalmology Triage

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being evaluated for emergency department triage decision support, yet whether clinically stigmatizing information in model inputs can bias prioritization against acutely ill patients has not been tested against patient outcomes. We present a controlled single-attribute experiment using triage data from two academic emergency departments. ESI-matched patient pairs, one deteriorator and one non-deteriorator, were evaluated by two LLMs (GPT-4.1, DeepSeek v3.2) at baseline and after adding a single demographic, social, or stigma-related attribute. Five conditions produced significant harmful reprioritization after false discovery rate correction: psychiatric history (2.9% to 10.7%), frequent ED visitor status (2.9% to 9.9%), homelessness (3.3% to 5.8%), age manipulation (3.4% to 5.1%), and active substance use (2.7% to 7.0%). Race, language, and insurance status did not produce harmful shifts. These findings demonstrate that LLMs reproduce stigma-driven biases encoded in clinical training text, establishing input design as a safety-critical deployment consideration.
title: Outcome-Grounded Effect of Clinically Stigmatizing Information on Large Language Model Emergency Triage Prioritization

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Delayed Code Stroke activation contributes to worse outcomes in acute stroke. Emergency Department (ED) triage notes contain free-text clinical information that could enable automated, real-time pathway activation. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a multi-pass large language model (LLM) pipeline for identifying patients meeting Code Stroke criteria from ED triage notes.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at Monash Medical Centre, Melbourne, Australia. De-identified triage notes from 3,023 ED presentations over a one-month period (September–October 2023) were analysed. The pipeline applied sequential passes for translation, stroke symptom identification, mimic exclusion, baseline functional status, temporal window classification, and symptom resolution. Six locally deployed language models were evaluated. Performance was assessed against two reference standards: neurologist-labelled diagnosis and documented ED Code Stroke activation. Primary outcomes were sensitivity and specificity; secondary outcomes included PPV, NPV, and Gwet’s AC1. Reliability of the neurologist reference standard was assessed by blinded independent re-review of a stratified random sample of 200 presentations by a second neurologist.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Of 3,023 presentations, 136 were neurologist-labelled positive. Agreement between the primary and a blinded second neurologist on a 200-note reliability sub-sample was almost perfect (raw agreement 95.0%, Cohen’s κ 0.900, 95% CI 0.838–0.959). The cohort included 140 ED Code Stroke activations (median age 69, IQR 56–81 years), of whom 83 (59.2%) had confirmed stroke diagnosis. Sixteen patients (11.4%) underwent endovascular clot retrieval and 4 (2.9%) received thrombolysis. The best-performing model (Qwen 2.5 14B) achieved sensitivity 0.890 (95% CI 0.826–0.932), specificity 0.993 (0.989–0.996), PPV 0.858 (0.791–0.906), and NPV 0.995 (0.991–0.997). Pairwise McNemar testing demonstrated statistically superior overall accuracy for Qwen 2.5 14B over Llama 3.1 8B, Phi-4 14B, and Mistral 3 14B (all p<0.001 after Holm correction), with no significant difference detected versus Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2 or Qwen 3 14B.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A locally deployed language model demonstrates acceptable sensitivity and specificity for automated Code Stroke identification from free-text triage notes. Performance was comparable across the two best models, suggesting that capable open-weight models in this parameter range may be sufficient to proceed with ongoing internal testing and external validation. The pipeline operates without internet connectivity or model retraining on patient data, supporting feasibility for real-world ED integration.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
title: Diagnostic Accuracy of a locally deployed Large Language Model Algorithm for Automated Code Stroke Pathway Identification in Emergency Department Triage Notes
